articles.title: Translations at Scale: Memory Optimization Techniques That Kept Uber's P99 Under 1ms
articles.summary: Uber profiles GC costs in a high-throughput Go translation library. It first replaces sync.Map with a value-based map and RWMutex, then introduces hybrid memory/disk caching to avoid reload-time OOMs. Sharded compact metadata, selective warmup, and a throttled LRU preserve over 99.9% cache hits while sharply reducing memory use.
articles.whyRead: Learn to distinguish GC object-count overhead from actual data size, and to revisit the bottleneck after every optimization. This is a practical lesson in choosing data structures for measured workload patterns, optimizing for access skew, and accounting for refresh-time memory peaks.

articles.title: BatchGen: An Architecture for Scalable and Efficient Batch Inference
articles.summary: BatchGen rethinks offline LLM inference around sequence coroutines that can yield, combine, partition, and migrate across a shared GPU pool. This addresses underfilled MoE expert batches and long-tail generation that leave GPUs idle under static placement. Its authors report up to 2.3x lower batch completion time on 128 GPUs.
articles.whyRead: Learn to question whether an execution model still matches its workload: interactive latency and full-batch completion time demand different scheduling. The transferable design move is to find natural yield points and movable work units, trading local scheduling overhead for higher global utilization and better straggler handling.

articles.title: Scaling AI in Legal: Building Uber's Redlining Agent
articles.summary: Uber describes how a contract-review agent evolved from unreliable playbook RAG into a hybrid system with clause-anchored policy rules, intent-indexed expert feedback, time-weighted examples, and a Word add-in. Deterministic rules override probabilistic recommendations, while lawyers retain final approval. Uber reports over 20% less average contract-review time.
articles.whyRead: Learn to build high-stakes agents around observed failure modes instead of a fashionable framework. Align retrieval keys with stable source documents; distinguish hard constraints from flexible judgments; and collect expert corrections as structured learning signals. The generalizable lesson is that reliable AI applications require deliberate boundaries between rules, model behavior, and human decisions.

articles.title: StriaTrace: Efficient Tracing and Diagnosis for Online LLM Inference (Operational Systems)
articles.summary: StriaTrace addresses intermittent tail-latency SLO violations in production LLM inference. Instead of expensive exhaustive profiling, it instruments key synchronization boundaries and critical paths, filters for anomalous executions, and uses a workload-aware performance model plus cross-layer correlation to identify root causes. The authors report under 1% overhead and diagnosis of 19 root-cause categories.
articles.whyRead: Develop a reusable observability instinct: trace the events that gate progress, not every function; follow the critical path; and preserve high-fidelity evidence when a dynamic workload deviates from its expected behavior. It shows why averages, static thresholds, and offline replay often miss transient failures in latency-sensitive distributed services.

articles.title: Designing MCP Gateway: Uber's MCP Management Platform
articles.summary: Uber describes the platform it built after ad-hoc MCP integrations stopped scaling: a centralized MCP Registry as the control plane and a Proxy Gateway as the data plane, translating agent tool calls into existing HTTP, gRPC, and TChannel services. The system now hosts more than 800 MCP servers and 5,000 tools while giving agents a consistent interface for discovery, execution, ownership, and governance.
articles.whyRead: The reusable idea is not MCP itself but how to introduce a fast-moving interface without forcing the whole backend estate to migrate at once. Uber puts a stable gateway in front of existing services, separates control plane from data plane, and treats tool discovery and governance as platform problems. It is a strong example of using translation layers and centralized metadata to scale a new abstraction across a large organization.

articles.title: How Databricks rolls out frontier models to 12,000 employees on Day 1
articles.summary: Databricks explains how it gives more than 12,000 employees immediate access to newly released frontier models without blindly making them defaults. Unity Gateway distributes model configuration, enforces per-user budgets, collects traces, and marks new models experimental while the team compares quality and cost over real workloads before promotion or removal.
articles.whyRead: This is a useful deployment pattern for any rapidly changing dependency: separate availability from promotion. Databricks can expose a new model on day one while bounding risk with budgets, observability, experimental labels, and a short evaluation window. The broader intuition is that fast adoption does not require skipping controls; good platform design can make experimentation cheap, reversible, and measurable.

articles.title: Taming the ML Firehose: Scaling Feature Consistency
articles.summary: Uber explains how it made online inference features the canonical source for future model training, eliminating training-serving skew while operating at recommendation traffic reaching 8 million QPS. The design spans selective feature logging, Kafka, Flink stream joins, state management, payload reduction, and multi-petabyte-scale cost constraints.
articles.whyRead: This is production ML engineering rather than model theory. The useful intuition is that ML correctness is often a data-systems problem: consistency, freshness, state, observability, and cost can matter as much as the model itself. It is also a concrete example of reducing an impossible-scale logging problem by asking which data actually has downstream value.

articles.title: An Organizational Second Brain: Building an AI That Learns From Experts
articles.summary: Meta describes an internal expert agent built around a structured knowledge layer, explicit reasoning procedures called recipes, automated evaluations, and a feedback loop that turns expert corrections into regression-tested updates without retraining the model.
articles.whyRead: The architectural lesson is unusually transferable: separate what an agent knows from how it reasons. That makes failures attributable, changes reviewable, and improvements testable. It is a useful blueprint for thinking about reliable agents as software systems built around an LLM rather than treating the model itself as the whole product.

articles.title: Scaling Managed Agents: Decoupling the brain from the hands
articles.summary: Anthropic explains the architecture behind Managed Agents for long-horizon work: separating the model and harness (the brain), execution environments and tools (the hands), and a durable session log. These interfaces let harnesses and sandboxes fail, scale, and evolve independently as model capabilities change.
articles.whyRead: A strong AI-systems lesson in designing abstractions around something that changes unusually fast. Instead of baking today's model limitations into infrastructure, Anthropic makes volatile components replaceable behind stable interfaces. It is a useful example of applying classic distributed-systems ideas—stateless workers, durable logs, failure isolation, and late resource provisioning—to agent infrastructure.

articles.title: Smaller, faster, safer: running Kimi and GLM at scale
articles.summary: Cloudflare describes how Workers AI serves large long-context models under GPU-memory constraints using FP8 KV-cache quantization, INT4 weight compression, disaggregated prefill and decode, and integrity checks for shared cache state. The post connects memory layout directly to concurrency, latency, throughput, cost, and reliability.
articles.whyRead: This is the kind of production AI infrastructure article worth learning from: an optimization is not simply 'faster' or 'smaller.' Prefill and decode have different bottlenecks, so the best representation differs by phase, and packing more work onto shared hardware creates new correctness risks. The broader intuition is to optimize around the actual bottleneck while accounting for the failure modes the optimization itself introduces.
